audience.programmeDescription: Utrecht’s Global Sustainability Science bachelor combines natural science, social science and research methods. Students begin with a shared foundation and then deepen their study through one of five tracks.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The Utrecht example follows Water, Climate & Ecosystems. The closest UCR option focuses on water, climate and ecology. The other two options explore sustainability through governance and social change, or through business, energy and resource use.

cellNotes.text: Both use interdisciplinary concepts to examine sustainability challenges. UCR introduces planetary boundaries and scientific tools through modelling and laboratory work.
Both develop mathematical tools for analysing systems. Utrecht embeds the tools in its sustainability programme.
Both study interactions among natural processes. UCR focuses on Earth systems, geology and field evidence.
Utrecht surveys social-science approaches to sustainability. UCR develops related perspectives across economics, governance and environmental justice courses.
Both develop research design and evidence skills. UCR adds statistical inference and quantitative analysis within this course.

Both integrate evidence and disciplinary perspectives in an applied sustainability project. Utrecht uses fieldwork and stakeholder research on Texel. UCR investigates sustainability campaigns. Take Research Skills GSS alongside the Utrecht project.
Both develop statistical inference and hypothesis testing. UCR gives greater emphasis to mathematical foundations and simulation. Utrecht requires full participation in Research Skills GSS first.

Both examine sustainability transitions, actors and possible interventions. Utrecht brings the perspectives together in a project. UCR focuses on governance and policy evaluation. Pass Research Skills GSS and the Regional Integration Project and participate fully in Statistics GSS before starting.
Both use chemistry to investigate environmental problems. UCR focuses on recovering materials and assessing remediation processes.
Both examine climate processes, impacts and possible responses. Utrecht deepens the topic within the track.
Utrecht requires a dedicated ecological field research course. UCR develops related field and laboratory skills in courses including Soils & Aquifers.

Both examine water in soils and related natural systems. UCR focuses on soils and shallow aquifers, while Utrecht integrates water and ecosystem processes. This advanced track course requires 90 EC and assumes prior study of environmental chemistry, global climate change and ecological field research.
Both examine biodiversity and ecological processes. Utrecht specialises in landscape ecology and conservation at advanced level.
Both examine chemical processes and contaminants in environmental systems. Utrecht gives additional attention to human exposure and health.

Before the 15 EC individual thesis, pass the specified common courses, the introductory and intermediate track requirements and at least one advanced major elective. Active participation is required in Statistics GSS, consultancy and the advanced track course. UCR’s optional independent research is separate from the scheduled courses.
The project works on an external organisation’s sustainability question. Entry requires at least 90 EC, including Sustainability Challenges and the two integration projects.
An example of the required choice between two intermediate major courses.
Choose 45 EC, with at least 15 EC at intermediate or advanced level. Options include extra major courses, a minor, study abroad or an internship. External courses require approval.

notes.text: Utrecht combines a 60 EC shared core with 75 EC of track requirements and major choices and a 45 EC optional course profile. Its separate ecological field research course, external consultancy project and individual thesis remain distinct features of this example.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

BENBUSI211.name: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
BENBUSI211.text: Examines AI's business, economic and societal implications without requiring a technical background. Students study AI's capabilities and limits, applications across business functions and industries, and effects on labour markets, productivity, innovation and inequality. Business cases and scholarly arguments support analysis of governance, regulation and a country's AI readiness and industrial policy.

BENECON312.name: Econometrics
BENECON312.text: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

ENSDELT312.name: Governance of Sustainability
ENSDELT312.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
